items.followUp: Describe the induced-fit model of enzyme action and write its equation.

rubric.why: Identifies how the substrate binds to the enzyme and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.description: Substrate binds at the enzyme’s active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the binding and complex formation.

rubric.why: Shows the reaction sequence and that the enzyme is available again after the reaction.
rubric.description: Gives the equation E + S ⇌ ES → E + P and indicates that the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation or an equivalent correctly labelled sequence.

modelAnswer: The substrate binds to the specific active site of an enzyme, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
The enzyme converts the substrate into product(s), which are released; the enzyme remains unchanged.
Equation: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P (E = enzyme, S = substrate, ES = enzyme-substrate complex, P = product).

items.followUp: State two differences between soluble and insoluble dietary fibres.

rubric.why: Identifies the key difference in solubility.
rubric.description: Insoluble dietary fibre does not dissolve in water, whereas soluble dietary fibre dissolves in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting their solubility.

rubric.why: Gives a valid function or example of insoluble fibre.
rubric.description: Insoluble fibre, such as cellulose, adds bulk to faeces and helps bowel movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct function or example of insoluble fibre.

rubric.why: This point is included within the two-mark comparison and is not separately scored.
rubric.description: Additional acceptable detail about soluble fibre.
rubric.how: Do not award an additional mark for this detail.

modelAnswer: Insoluble dietary fibre, such as cellulose, does not dissolve in water; it adds bulk to faeces and helps movement through the intestine.
Soluble dietary fibre, such as pectin, dissolves in water and may form a gel; it can slow the absorption of nutrients.

items.followUp: Name the two types of agranulocytes and state one function of each.

rubric.why: Names one correct type of agranulocyte.
rubric.description: Lymphocytes are a type of agranulocyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming lymphocytes.

rubric.why: Names the other correct type of agranulocyte.
rubric.description: Monocytes are the other type of agranulocyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming monocytes.

modelAnswer: Agranulocytes are white blood cells whose cytoplasm does not contain visible granules.
Their two types are lymphocytes and monocytes.

items.followUp: Describe the structure of the pericardium and explain how it protects the heart.

rubric.why: Describes the pericardium as a membrane surrounding the heart.
rubric.description: The pericardium is a double-walled sac or membrane surrounding the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a double membrane or sac around the heart.

rubric.why: Explains a protective function of the pericardium.
rubric.description: Pericardial fluid reduces friction as the heart beats; the sac also helps protect and hold the heart in place.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct protective function.

modelAnswer: The pericardium is a double-walled sac surrounding the heart.
The fluid between its walls reduces friction as the heart beats, and the sac helps protect the heart and hold it in position.

items.followUp: Explain the cell and organ levels of biological organization, giving an example of each.

rubric.why: Explains that organelles are specialized cell structures and identifies their role or examples.
rubric.description: At the organelle level, specialized structures within a cell perform particular functions; examples include mitochondria and ribosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the level and 1 mark for a valid example or function.

rubric.why: Explains that tissues are groups of similar cells working together and gives a valid example.
rubric.description: At the tissue level, similar cells work together to perform a particular function; examples include muscle and epithelial tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the level and 1 mark for a valid example.

modelAnswer: At the organelle level, specialized structures within a cell perform particular functions; for example, mitochondria release energy and ribosomes make proteins.
At the tissue level, a group of similar cells works together to perform a particular function; muscle tissue, for example, contracts to produce movement.

items.followUp: Define plastids and describe the functions of chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts.

rubric.why: Defines plastids as organelles found in plant cells and gives a relevant structural or functional feature.
rubric.description: Plastids are double-membraned organelles in plant cells, often containing pigments or storing food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Identifies the green plastid and its function.
rubric.description: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the chloroplast and its function.

rubric.why: Identifies chromoplasts and their pigment or colour function.
rubric.description: Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments and give colour to parts such as flowers and fruits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description of chromoplasts.

rubric.why: Identifies leucoplasts and their storage role.
rubric.description: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food, such as starch, oils or proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description of leucoplasts.

rubric.why: Requires a labelled diagram showing all three types of plastid.
rubric.description: Draws a classification diagram showing plastids divided into chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear, correctly labelled diagram containing all three types.

modelAnswer: Plastids are double-membraned organelles in plant cells; they contain pigments or store food.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments and give colour to flowers and fruits.
Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food such as starch, oils or proteins.

Diagram construction: draw one top box 4 cm wide × 1.5 cm high and label it “Plastids”; draw three boxes, each 3 cm wide × 1.5 cm high, in a row below it; connect the top box to each lower box with a line and label the lower boxes “Chloroplast”, “Chromoplast” and “Leucoplast”.

items.followUp: Name the scientist who proposed the five-kingdom system and give two characteristics of each of two kingdoms in it.

rubric.why: Names the scientist who proposed the five-kingdom system.
rubric.description: The five-kingdom system was proposed by Robert Whittaker.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Robert Whittaker.

rubric.why: Gives valid characteristics or examples of Protista.
rubric.description: Protista consists mainly of unicellular eukaryotes; many live in water, and examples include Amoeba and Paramecium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of Protista.

rubric.why: Describes fungi using valid characteristics of their cells, nutrition or structure.
rubric.description: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs that absorb nutrients; most are multicellular, have chitin cell walls and grow as hyphae forming a mycelium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct characteristic and 1 mark for another characteristic or a valid example.

modelAnswer: The five-kingdom system was proposed by Robert Whittaker in 1969.
Kingdom Protista includes mostly unicellular eukaryotes; many are aquatic, and they may be autotrophic or heterotrophic. Examples include Amoeba and Paramecium.

Kingdom Fungi consists of eukaryotic heterotrophs that absorb nutrients from their surroundings; most are multicellular, have chitin cell walls and form thread-like hyphae that make a mycelium. Yeast is a unicellular fungus.

items.followUp: Explain how food is mechanically and chemically digested in the mouth.

rubric.why: Identifies chewing by the teeth as mechanical digestion in the oral cavity.
rubric.description: Teeth chew food into smaller pieces, mechanically digesting it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the role of the teeth or chewing.

rubric.why: Explains how saliva prepares food for swallowing.
rubric.description: Saliva moistens and lubricates food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct role of saliva.

rubric.why: Identifies the chemical action of salivary amylase.
rubric.description: Salivary amylase begins the digestion of starch, producing maltose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct enzyme, substrate and product.

rubric.why: Explains the tongue’s role in mixing food and forming a bolus for swallowing.
rubric.description: The tongue mixes food with saliva, forms it into a bolus and helps push it back for swallowing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct role of the tongue or bolus formation.

modelAnswer: The teeth chew food into smaller pieces, carrying out mechanical digestion.
Saliva moistens and lubricates the food.
Salivary amylase begins the chemical digestion of starch into maltose.
The tongue mixes the food with saliva, forms it into a bolus and pushes it back for swallowing.
